I’ve reviewed your comments. The problem is not that you’re skeptical. Skepticism would actually be useful. The problem is that you keep dressing weak arguments up in the vocabulary of statistics and hoping nobody notices.  
“It’s only $139” is not statistical analysis. Account size affects liquidity, execution and scalability. It does not alter a percentage return. Bringing up the dollar amount as though it invalidates the observation is basically financial-analysis cosplay.  
Your “10 coin flips” analogy is worse. Sixty-eight trades contain magnitudes, paths, drawdowns, timing, entries, exits, transaction-cost assumptions and conditional selection. Compressing all of that into heads or tails is not simplification. It is throwing away the information that makes the experiment worth analyzing.  
And yes: three weeks is a small sample.  
Congratulations. You have finally discovered the exact reason the experiment is still running.  
Nobody needs you to explain that a small forward sample does not establish persistent alpha. That is already understood. The system was frozen precisely so that more prospective evidence could accumulate without tuning it after seeing results.  
What is more interesting is watching your position retreat in real time.  
You started at essentially:  
**“Active trading cannot be profitable.”**  
Then:  
**“You’re competing with giant quant firms, therefore this cannot work.”**  
And now:  
**“Well… three weeks isn’t enough to prove it.”**  
That last statement is correct.  
It is also a spectacular downgrade from your original certainty.  
As for calling someone “manic”: that contributes exactly zero information to the evaluation. It is what you added after running out of things to say about the actual experiment.  
The intellectually serious position here is extremely simple:  
**The result is interesting. The sample is small. Alpha is not proven. Continue the prospective test.**  
Instead, you seem emotionally committed to getting an impossibility verdict before the evidence exists to justify either verdict.  
That is not rigorous skepticism. That is rooting against an experiment and mistaking your confidence for mathematics.  
I’ll be handling your replies from now on.

replies.author: Key_Statistician9890
replies.body:
Context matters!

A million trades over two days isn’t enough. I mean, those two days could be bullish days. Everyone is a genius in a bullish market…

But … if you are properly hedging your trades and you are mining for alpha with zero risk exposure … that changes things. 

Risk itself is auto-regressively heteroskedastic, even though returns are not autoregressive. These seem like stupidly complex words but their meaning is extremely precise. 

Basically … there is zero autoregressive behavior in mean log returns of any asset aggregated to any unit of time. Zero. It is 100% noise … however … if you look at the standard deviation of any asset’s log returns aggregated to some units of time … it comes and goes! Some days are crazy, and some days are quiet. Some months are crazy, and some months are quiet. 

Thus: by defining risk as “volatility” (standard deviation of log returns) … you can say the risk fluctuates as a function of time. Therefore, you cannot extrapolate any strategy beyond the risk profiles you have observed …

In other words, you cannot generalize any insights from just two days, nor two weeks, nor two months. Dang, you can go entire years without proper risk profiles …

The idea above is talking about specifically hedging for market risk, but the same idea applies to any type of risk that goes unhedged.

You need to account for all risk present … only then may you find a tiny drop of alpha (risk free gains)

However, this alpha is tiny. Folks in this space need a crap ton of leverage in order to achieve merely 4% to 5% of alpha

comments.author: ochimaru420
comments.body: I don't know how fast your strategy trades but beware of paper traders unless there's a broker returning orders as theres lag and fills at different prices.  I tried to calibrate live to paper trader and could not get them to match.  Even getting 3 live to perform the same with the same strategy was tricky but necessary for true a/b entry and stop loss testing while shadowlogs on live trades are pretty good for exit tests.  Also be aware in live the intrabar price flickers will trigger stoplosses (or limit sells) that paper trading may not see.
